power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Mediterranean-style dietary components and self-reported depression: a crosssectional analysis of 502,359 UK adults in the UK Biobank cohort

author.affiliation:
School of Health and Wellbeing
								University of Glasgow
								
									Glasgow
									UK

text.text: Background: Mediterranean-style diet adherence has been associated with lower depression prevalence, but studies are typically small and adjust for few confounders.

We aimed to estimate cross-sectional associations between individual Mediterraneanstyle dietary components and reported depression, and how far they attenuate with broader sociodemographic and lifestyle adjustment.
Methods: Cross-sectional analysis of the UK Biobank cohort (N=502,359).

Six selfreported dietary variables -oily fish, non-oily fish, fresh fruit, salad and raw vegetables, cooked vegetables and processed meat -were tested against self-reported depression using binary logistic regression, modelled individually with progressive adjustment (full adjustment: age, sex, smoking, medication, Townsend deprivation index, month of assessment, educational attainment), then all together in one multivariable model.
Results: 28,194 participants (5.6%) reported depression.

Fully adjusted, higher intakes of oily fish (odds ratio[OR]=0.900, 95% CI [confidence intervals] 0.888 to 0.912), nonoily fish (OR=0.931, 0.917 to 0.945), fresh fruit (OR=0.974, 0.966 to 0.982), salad and raw vegetables (OR=0.970, 0.964 to 0.976) and cooked vegetables (OR=0.967, 0.960 to 0.974) were each associated with lower odds.
Conclusion: Individual components of a Mediterranean-style diet showed small, consistent associations with lower odds of self-reported depression, not explained by the measured confounders.
The design does not support causal interpretation.

For researchers, prospective designs with repeated dietary measurement and diagnosed outcomes are needed; for practitioners and policymakers, these estimates do not support dietary components as a substitute for established treatment or as a standalone prevention target.

Greater adherence to a Mediterranean-style diet has been associated with lower depression prevalence, but the evidence rests largely on modest samples with limited adjustment for socioeconomic deprivation, educational attainment and seasonality.

In more than half a million UK adults, associations between individual Mediterraneanstyle dietary items and lower odds of reported depression persisted after adjustment for that broader confounder set, but the estimates were small: the largest, for oily fish, corresponded to approximately 10% lower odds per category of weekly intake, and the fruit and vegetable estimates were around 3% per daily portion.

Processed meat intake, expected on prior evidence to associate with higher odds of depression, showed at most a small association with higher risk once age and sex were accounted for, and none on multivariable adjustment for the other dietary components.

The persistence of small associations across a broad confounder set justifies prospective work using repeated dietary measurement and diagnosed outcomes, but the magnitudes observed do not support dietary components as a substitute for established treatment or as a stand-alone target for depression prevention policy.
Depression is among the leading contributors to global disability, affecting approximately 322 million people worldwide.
¹ Available pharmacological treatments are effective for many patients but have a delayed onset of action,² and adverse effects are a common reason for discontinuation.
³ ⁴ There is therefore continuing interest in modifiable lifestyle exposures -diet in particular -that might contribute to prevention at population level and are inexpensive and broadly acceptable.

⁵ The Mediterranean-style dietary pattern, characterised by high intakes of fruit, vegetables, legumes, fish and olive oil, moderate alcohol intake and limited red and processed meat,⁶ has been associated with lower incidence of cardiovascular disease⁷ ⁸ and, in a number of cohorts, with lower depression prevalence and incidence.

⁹ ¹⁰ ¹¹ ¹² ¹³ ¹⁴ ¹⁵ The SMILES trial reported a reduction in depressive symptoms following a modified Mediterranean dietary intervention in adults with major depression,¹⁶ although its recruitment practices and effect size have been questioned,¹⁷ and the PREDIMED substudy did not find a significant reduction in depression incidence overall.
¹⁸ A further Mediterranean-style intervention supplemented with fish oil improved both diet quality and mental health in adults with depression.
¹⁹ Two features of the existing observational literature limit its interpretation.
First, sample sizes are typically modest, so precision is limited and small effects cannot reliably be distinguished from null.
Second, adjustment for confounding is usually partial.

Depression prevalence varies with age and sex,²⁰ ²¹ socioeconomic deprivation,²² educational attainment,²³ smoking²⁴ ²⁵ and season of assessment,²⁶ ²⁷ and each of these also plausibly relates to diet.

Where they are not modelled jointly, an apparent diet-depression association may reflect the broader socioeconomic and behavioural context in which Mediterranean-style eating occurs rather than diet itself.

We used the UK Biobank cohort²⁸ to test cross-sectional associations between six self-reported dietary intake variables corresponding to components of a Mediterranean-style pattern and self-reported depression.

Our aim was to establish whether any association survives simultaneous adjustment for a broader confounder set than has typically been applied, and to quantify the magnitude of any residual association.
Fully adjusted models are reported in the main text; unadjusted and partially adjusted models are provided as supplementary material.

Six baseline touchscreen dietary variables were examined, selected to correspond to components of a Mediterranean-style pattern: oily fish intake, non-oily fish intake, fresh fruit intake, salad and raw vegetable intake, cooked vegetable intake, and processed meat intake.
Fish and processed meat intake were reported on a six-level ordinal frequency scale ('never', 'less than once a week', 'once a week', '2-4 times a week', '5-6 times a week', 'once or more daily').
Fruit and vegetable intake were reported as pieces or heaped tablespoons consumed per day.
Responses of 'do not know' or 'prefer not to answer' were set to missing.
For the fruit and vegetable items, responses of 'less than one' were coded as 0.5.
No dietary variable was categorised or dichotomised; each was entered on its original scale.

Processed meat was included as a component expected to show the opposite direction of association, since it is not a feature of the Mediterranean pattern and higher intake has been associated with incident depression in other cohorts³⁰ and with type 2 diabetes.

³¹ Because the intake variables are recorded on different scales, odds ratios are not directly comparable across components: a one-unit difference represents one category of weekly frequency for the fish and meat variables, and one portion per day for the fruit and vegetable variables.
Estimates should be read within, not across, components.
UK Biobank does not record olive oil or nut consumption, both central to the Mediterranean pattern, nor does it capture food quality or preparation.
We therefore did not derive a composite Mediterranean diet adherence score, and each component was modelled individually.
The analysis should be read as a test of individual dietary components rather than of adherence to a dietary pattern.
Depression was defined by participant self-report at baseline (yes/no), recorded at the nurse-led verbal interview.
Age at assessment in years and self-reported sex were treated as confounders, both being related to dietary intake and to depression prevalence.
²⁰ ²¹ Smoking status (ever versus never) was treated as a confounder given its established associations with both diet and depression.

²⁴ ²⁵ Socioeconomic position was captured on two axes of inequality: area-level deprivation, using the Townsend Deprivation Index derived from postcode of residence from aggregated data on car ownership, household overcrowding, owner occupation and unemployment,³² and individual educational attainment, binarised as possession of a college or university degree.
Both were treated as confounders.
²² ²³ Month of assessment was included as a 12-level categorical variable (January as reference) to account for seasonal variation in reported mood documented in this cohort.

²⁶ Medication use was recorded at the touchscreen as use of cholesterol-lowering medication, blood pressure medication or insulin and, in women, hormone replacement therapy or the oral contraceptive pill, and was binarised as any versus none.
This was treated as a broad marker of regular medication use and physical health.
The analytic sample comprised N= 502,359 participants.

Item-level missingness was low: below 2% for each of the six dietary variables (n available 494,512 to 500,128), 0.1% for Townsend deprivation, 0.8% for medication, 0.6% for smoking status and 1.1% for educational attainment.
Analyses were complete-case with respect to the variables entered in each model.
The multivariable model included 477,181 participants (95.0%), of whom 26,588 reported depression.

Given the low proportion missing on any single variable, multiple imputation was not undertaken; complete-case analysis nonetheless assumes that missingness is unrelated to the outcome conditional on the covariates, which we cannot verify.
Associations between each dietary variable and depression were estimated using binary logistic regression.

Each dietary component was modelled individually at four levels of adjustment: unadjusted; model 1, adjusted for age and sex; model 2, additionally adjusted for smoking status and medication; and model 3 (fully adjusted), additionally adjusted for Townsend deprivation, month of assessment and educational attainment.
A fifth, multivariable model entered all six dietary components and all covariates simultaneously, so that each dietary estimate is mutually adjusted for the others.
Adding covariates in steps allows the point at which an estimate attenuates to be identified.
³³.
We report ORs with 95% confidence intervals.
Coefficients for the covariates in the multivariable model are reported in supplementary table S4.

text.text: Processed meat intake showed the opposite pattern to that expected before adjustment, being associated with lower odds of depression (OR=0.961, 95% CI 0.950 to 0.972); this reversed direction on adjustment for age and sex (OR=1.023, 95% CI 1.011 to 1.036), and attenuated with each further level of adjustment, becoming non-significant in the multivariable model.
This pattern is consistent with confounding by age and sex rather than with a robust dietary association.

In a general-population cohort of over 500,000 adults, higher self-reported intakes of oily fish, non-oily fish, fresh fruit, salad and cooked vegetables were each associated with modestly lower odds of self-reported depression.

These estimates persisted after simultaneous adjustment for age, sex, smoking status, medication, area deprivation, educational attainment and month of assessment, and after mutual adjustment for the other dietary components.
Processed meat intake showed at most a small association with higher odds of depression once age and sex were accounted for, and none on mutual adjustment for the other dietary components.
The direction of these findings is consistent with meta-analyses of dietary indices and depressive outcomes⁹ and with cohort studies of Mediterranean adherence.

¹¹ ¹² ¹³ ¹⁴ The contribution here is not the direction but the robustness of the estimates to adjustment: they were not explained by the confounders most often cited as alternative explanations, and in particular their persistence after adjustment for month of assessment suggests they do not simply reflect seasonal covariation of mood and eating, which has been documented in this cohort.

²⁶ Against this, the estimates are small in absolute terms, and the attenuation seen on mutual adjustment indicates that participants who report higher oily fish intake also tend to report higher vegetable intake, so the individual estimates should not be summed or read as independent contributions.

Mechanistic accounts have been proposed -long-chain omega-3 fatty acids,³⁴ polyphenol and antioxidant content,³⁵ ³⁶ and gut-brain signalling³⁷ -but the present data cannot discriminate among them, and the estimates are equally compatible with residual confounding by health-conscious behaviour, general physical health or personality traits related to both diet and mood.

³⁸ The principal strengths of this analysis are the size and phenotypic depth of the cohort, which allow precise estimation and joint adjustment for a wider confounder set than is usual in this literature, and the stepwise presentation, which makes the point of attenuation visible rather than reporting a single adjusted model.
There are limitations however.

The design is cross-sectional, so exposure and outcome were measured at the same visit; temporal ordering cannot be established, and reverse causation is plausible given that depression alters appetite and food choice.

The outcome is self-reported rather than assessed against diagnostic criteria,³⁹ which will misclassify both low mood without disorder and undiagnosed depression; the observed prevalence of 5.6% is lower than most community estimates, which suggests under-ascertainment and, if differential with respect to diet, could bias estimates in either direction.

The exposures are self-reported single-item frequency measures rather than validated dietary records, and are subject to recall and social-desirability bias; because they are recorded on different scales, the estimates are not comparable across components.
The exposure set also does not represent the Mediterranean diet.

Olive oil, nuts and wine are absent from the baseline touchscreen and no composite adherence score could be constructed, so the components tested are better described as markers of a broadly healthier diet than as indices of Mediterranean adherence.

The adjustment set was specified from the literature rather than from an explicit causal diagram, and omits total energy intake, body mass index, physical activity, alcohol intake, comorbid physical illness and genetic liability to depression,⁴⁰ any of which could account for part of what we observe; residual and unmeasured confounding is therefore likely, and we did not undertake quantitative bias analysis to bound it.

Finally, UK Biobank is not representative of the UK population: the participation rate was 5.5%, and participants are on average healthier, less deprived and better educated than the general population,⁴¹ which limits generalisability, particularly to more deprived groups and to those with existing illness, and would be expected to attenuate rather than inflate the estimates.
The baseline age range also excludes younger adults, among whom incidence is high.
For practice and policy, these findings do not necessarily warrant dietary recommendation for depression prevention.

The estimates are small, cross-sectional and derived from a sample which is not necessarily generalizable to the general population; they are consistent with a modest contribution of diet to population-level variation in reported depression, but they cannot distinguish that from confounding by the wider circumstances in which healthier eating occurs, and dietary change should not be presented to patients as an alternative to established treatment.
They may reasonably inform the design of prevention research rather than prevention itself.

For research, the priorities are prospective analysis with repeated dietary assessment and diagnosed depression outcomes, construction of a validated adherence score in cohorts that capture olive oil, nut and alcohol intake, explicit specification of the causal structure through a directed acyclic graph, and quantitative bias analysis to assess how much unmeasured confounding would be required to explain estimates of this size.
Triangulation with designs carrying different assumptions, including Mendelian randomisation, would be informative.

In summary, individual components of a Mediterranean-style dietary pattern showed small, consistent cross-sectional associations with lower odds of self-reported depression in UK Biobank, which were not explained by age, sex, smoking, medication, deprivation, education or season of assessment.
The associations are compatible with a modest protective contribution of diet, but equally with residual confounding or reverse causation, and their magnitude is small.
Prospective analyses using repeated dietary assessment and diagnosed outcomes are required before any dietary recommendation for depression prevention could be supported.

Design, setting and participants UK Biobank is a general-population cohort of over 500,000 participants recruited to 22 assessment centres across England, Wales and Scotland between 2006 and 2010, aged approximately 40 to 70 years at baseline.
²⁸ ²⁹ Participants completed touchscreen questionnaires, a verbal interview, physical measurements and biological sampling.
This is a cross-sectional analysis of baseline data: exposures and outcome were recorded at the same visit.
Analyses were completed under project #17689.
Reporting follows the STROBE statement for cross-sectional studies.
We estimate the cross-sectional association between each of six dietary intake variables and reported depression.
UK Biobank holds generic ethical approval from the NHS National Research Ethics Service (ref.
11/NW/0382, 17 June 2011), all participants gave written informed consent, and the research conformed to the principles embodied in the Declaration of Helsinki.
